abstract: Generative structure-prediction models can directly predict protein-ligand complexes from sequence and ligand information, but their ability to capture pharmacologically relevant kinase-inhibitor interactions remains incompletely understood. We systematically evaluated Boltz-2 using curated biochemical IC50 measurements across eight human kinases, nine clinically used inhibitors, and representative resistance mutations. Although predicted log10(IC50) values showed a compressed dynamic range relative to experimental measurements, mutation-dependent shifts in inhibitor sensitivity, inhibitor selectivity patterns, and overall potency rankings showed substantial agreement with the experimental patterns within the present benchmark. Predicted binding probability showed good discrimination between binder and non-binder pairs within the present benchmark and a consistent inverse relationship with experimental potency. Structural analyses showed that ligand-pose variability was associated with prediction behavior within the evaluated kinase-inhibitor systems, even when kinase-domain structures showed close agreement with the corresponding experimental structures. Larger ligand RMSD values were not associated with larger prediction errors in magnitude, but were linked to systematic shifts in prediction bias, indicating that ligand-pose accuracy and predictive utility are not equivalent measures of Boltz-2 performance. These findings suggest that, within the present benchmark, relative kinase-inhibitor interaction patterns were reproduced more consistently than absolute potency values. We provide a framework for interpreting Boltz-2 outputs within the kinase-inhibitor systems examined here.

abstract: Abstract Epithelial tissues serve as critical physical barriers that protect organs, making their efficient repair essential upon damage. To achieve this, tissues must quickly react, forcing cells to rearrange and accommodate to achieve rapid wound closure. In the Drosophila wing disc, we previously showed how tissue fluidisation accelerated wound healing in 2D. However, the 3D aspect of tissue repair remains poorly understood. Here, we uncover a new mechanism that facilitates tissue repair through changing cell height. We find actomyosin contractile cables at the wound edge connecting the apical and basal cell surfaces, which indent the apical side of the tissue and deform the basement membrane, respectively. To assess the role of the different repair mechanisms, we develop a 3D vertex model allowing independent apical, lateral and basal behaviours. The model predicts that lateral cables play a role in regulating planar cell-cell intercalations, confirmed by Drosophila mutations affecting cell deformations. Our results demonstrate that lateral cables cooperate with the apical purse string to drive 3D cell shape changes and planar cell-cell intercalations for efficient wound repair.

abstract: We present MUFASA (Multi-Protocol Unified Fluorescence-based Advanced Simulation Algorithm), a physically grounded, continuous-time simulator of several super-resolution fluorescence microscopy protocols. By modeling fluorophore dynamics using continuous-time Markov chains, MUFASA’s simulation features yield realistic photon emission behavior across both Single Molecule Localization Microscopy (SMLM) and fluorescence fluctuation-based (FF-SRM) settings–independently of frame duration and sampling. The framework supports both individual emitters and structure-level simulations, incorporating photophysical transitions, photobleaching, and camera properties.To quantitatively compare simulations with real data, we introduce a novel validation metric based on the 1-Wasserstein distance between simulated and experimental photon-count distributions. Another functionality of MUFASA is the estimation of key photophysical parameters (e.g., molar extinction coefficient) and the suggestion of optimal light-source power ranges from fluctuation data.An intuitive Python-based graphical interface for real-time parameter tuning, visualization, and TIFF export is provided.Designed for biologists, physicists, microscopists, and computational imaging engineers, MUFASA offers a practical platform for microscopy experiment design, hypothesis testing and holds the potential of being used for the generation of realistic training data for data-driven methods across modalities.

abstract: In this study, the differential interaction mechanism of curcumin with the lipid/Chol monolayer (molar ratio 7:3) rich in electrically neutral PC groups and rich in negatively charged PS groups was revealed at the membrane level. Using the Langmuir monolayer technique combined with atomic force microscopy, the effects of different concentrations of curcumin (22, 41, 253 ng/mL) on the surface pressure-mean molecular area isotherms, elastic modulus, relaxation time, and microscopic morphology of the two mixed monolayers were systematically studied. The results showed that the interaction strength between curcumin and the POPS/Chol monolayer was significantly greater than that of the POPC/Chol monolayer, and the response pattern was quite different. The AFM results further shown that curcumin may be adsorbed in the form of aggregates in POPC/Chol monolayer films, while no curcumin aggregates were observed in POPS/Chol monolayer films. The above difference are most likely due to the negative charge of the PS head group and its high exposure on the surface of the monolayer, allowing curcumin to interact with it more strongly through ion-dipole interaction.This study revealed a new mechanism of curcumin’s anti-tumor selectivity at the level of the membrane and provided experimental evidence for designing curcumin delivery strategies targeting the characteristics of tumor membrane phospholipids.

abstract: Photobiomodulation outcomes depend on how light delivery, tissue heating, and cellular energy-related activity change together. This study develops a three-dimensional computational framework that combines light transport, heat transfer, and a phenomenological model of adenosine triphosphate-related activity in layered skin, fat, and skeletal muscle. The model compares wavelengths of 810, 850, and 900 nm and evaluates the effects of optical power, beam radius, and a 180 s exposure period. Under the common optical condition, 900 nm produces the highest average and maximum light levels in muscle, whereas 850 nm provides an intermediate response and is retained as a representative wavelength for the coupled analyses. Increasing the beam radius markedly reduces local light concentration near the tissue surface while producing little change in the average light level within muscle. At 850 nm with a Gaussian $$1/e^2$$ beam radius of $$w=4$$ mm, the modeled muscle-averaged ATP-related response increases at low optical power, reaches a near-flat maximum of approximately 14.73% between 0.50 and 0.75 W, and then gradually decreases to approximately 12.29% at 2.50 W. In contrast, maximum tissue temperature and cumulative thermal exposure increase continuously with optical power. At 0.75 W, the maximum temperature is 38.584 $$^\circ \textrm{C}$$, while at 2.50 W it rises to 45.857 $$^\circ \textrm{C}$$. A local sensitivity analysis further shows that the magnitude and location of the modeled response maximum depend on the selected inhibition threshold. The results show that greater light delivery does not necessarily produce a greater modeled cellular energy response and may instead increase thermal loading. The framework supports comparison of coupled optical, thermal, and biological trends, but its predictions remain conditional on the selected tissue properties, geometry, and phenomenological parameters. Experimental measurements and higher-fidelity light-transport models are required before quantitative physiological or clinical interpretation.

abstract: Abstract The transcription factor Bicoid (Bcd) protein guides early Drosophila patterning and is the best-characterised morphogen. The source of the morphogen, bcd mRNA, is maternally deposited during oogenesis and localised to the anterior pole. When and where Bcd protein is produced and how this protein gradient is dynamically shaped remains contentious. Here, we use the SunTag reporter system to quantitatively examine the spatiotemporal profile of bcd mRNA translation in vivo. We show that association with Processing bodies (P bodies) in mature oocytes prevent premature bcd mRNA translation. Following egg activation, bcd mRNA dissociates from P bodies and translation is observed at the anterior pole. Translation remains largely restricted to the anterior domain throughout early development. At cellularisation, translation ceases and the remaining bcd mRNA associates with reformed P bodies, which appear to block any further translation. We use these observations to create a new modified synthesis-diffusion-degradation model of Bcd gradient, which is consistent with experimental measurements. Overall, our study reveals that bcd mRNA translation is tightly controlled in space and time during oogenesis and early embryogenesis.

abstract: Schwann cells are vital to development and maintenance of the peripheral nervous system, and their dysfunction has been implicated in a range of neurological and neoplastic disorders, including NF2-related schwannomatosis (NF2-SWN). We have developed a human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) model for the study of Schwann-like cell differentiation in health and disease. We performed sequence-based transcriptomics, immunofluorescence-based morphological analysis, and CRISPR-Cas9-based validation of differentiation from hiPSCs derived Schwann cell precursors (SCPs) to terminally differentiated Schwann-like cells (SLCs) representing 6 distinct stages of development across a period of 31 days. To further validate our findings, we performed integrated, cross-species analyses at bulk and single cell resolution. Our hiPSCs model of Schwann cell development shared overlapping gene expression signatures with human amniotic mesenchymal stem cell (hAMSCs) derived SLCs and in vivo mouse models but also revealed unique features that may reflect species-specific aspects of Schwann cell biology. Moreover, we have identified gene co-expression modules that are dynamically regulated during hiPSCs to SLCs differentiation associated with ear and neural development, cell fate determination, the NF2 gene, and extracellular matrix (ECM) organization. Through integrated analysis of multiple datasets and genetic disruption of NF2 via CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing in hiPSC derived SCPs, we have identified transcriptomic signatures suggesting a series of novel ECM associated genes potentially regulated by Merlin, providing a hypothesis-generating framework for future functional studies. The hiPSC model generated in this study further provides a system for studying NF2-regulated gene expression throughout Schwann-like cell development in the context of widely available data on iPSC Schwann cells and rare diseases that lack effective treatments such as NF2-SWN.

abstract: The prevailing view holds that simpler animate beings predating the dawn of cellular life once existed, yet they have long since vanished from the present-day Earth. Our hypothesis posits that these animate beings persist to this day. To this end, we devised a long-term experiment spanning over a decade, keeping Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) within a sealed aqueous system of pure water. The findings illustrated that, upon the complete cell death (CCD) of the S. aureus, as cellular remnants progressively succumbed to dissolution, the aqueous solution underwent self-purification, bringing forth a class of lipid bilayer membrane microspheres containing RNA and proteins. These structures maintained long-term sustainable stability within the thermodynamic storm of water molecules and underwent dynamic size fluctuations over time - collectively exhibited phenomena indicative of being "alive". This study reveals that the cell, upon complete cell death, undergoes reversion to a living entity simpler than the cell itself - the Meta Body (MB). The discovery of MB opens an entire re-conceptualization of what death ultimately brings.

abstract: Ion-pairs are central charged motifs that control the biological function of several proteins. Yet, the physical principles linked to the formation of ion-pairs during protein folding remain poorly understood. Here, we show that buried ion-pairs of de novo-designed helical bundle proteins reshape the folding pathways by introducing kinetic barriers that are overcome by a hydrophobic collapse linked to packing of the protein core. By combining protein design with co-translational folding studies, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, and molecular dynamics simulations, we show that introduction of a buried ion-pair leads to a shifted folding transition that balances desolvation and electrostatic interactions within the protein and the bulk solvent. Moreover, we find that the folding pathway is sensitive to modifications in non-polar interactions and motifs that electrostatically shield the ion-pair from its surroundings. Our combined findings provide a blueprint for understanding how functional motifs affect protein folding and how mutation of charged networks alter the stability of proteins.

abstract: Production of glycoconjugate vaccines has long relied upon chemical methods which are highly complex and expensive, resulting in vaccines that are not widely affordable. Heterologous bioconjugation methods, such as Protein-Glycan Coupling Technology (PGCT), have emerged as a path to significantly cheaper manufacture using safe host organisms, such as Escherichia coli, for recombinant glycoconjugate expression. PGCT glycoconjugate synthesis components are typically encoded across three plasmids and require the addition of exogenous chemical inducers for gene expression. In this study, we utilise modular DNA assembly to generate a single constitutive plasmid for biosynthesis of a Streptococcus pyogenes rhamnose polysaccharide glycoconjugate vaccine. This approach resulted in a greater than seven-fold glycoconjugate yield as well as simplified cell culture conditions compared to the traditional three plasmid inducible system. Importantly, given the modular nature of this method, this innovation could be applied to the manufacture of glycoconjugate vaccines against a range of pathogens.

abstract: We investigate the rate of change of equilibrium potential energy for nonlinear elastic solids undergoing evolutions that may involve changes in body geometry, material properties, applied tractions, and prescribed displacements. We represent such an evolution by a one-parameter family of variational problems and identify a class of these families for which the potential-energy release rate is well defined. Particular attention is given to the formulation of the potential energy at each evolution state: each constituent variational problem must yield the appropriate equilibrium state, while its equilibrium value must also correctly represent the physical change in potential energy between states. Within this framework, we derive a closed-form expression for the potential-energy release rate for solids with bounded domains, allowing for spatially nonuniform material evolution, sharp material interfaces, and evolving boundary geometry and prescribed boundary data. The expression is determined entirely by the equilibrium solution at the state under consideration and by the quantities prescribing the local evolution, so neighboring equilibrium problems need not be solved. Finally, we apply the result to the extension of a notch in a two-dimensional elastic body and show that the resulting potential-energy release rate reduces to the classical $J$-integral.

abstract: Frustration generated by competing interactions can stabilise patterns with tunable lengthscales which evade indefinite coarsening and macroscopic phase separation. Here we investigate a charged binary fluid in which the tendency toward phase separation is opposed by screened electrostatic repulsion. Combining analytics and numerical simulations, we identify a regime of arrested phase separation characterised by finite-wavelength instability. The resulting states include droplet and labyrinthine phases in two dimensions, and droplets, concentric shells and tubular structures in three dimensions. Surprisingly, some of these structures are amorphous morphologies that emerge reproducibly from different initial conditions. Free-energy estimates suggest that these disordered structures may be thermodynamically stabilised by frustration, rather than being kinetically trapped. Our results identify a simple mechanism through which the competition between phase separation and screened electrostatics can generate equilibrium amorphous microphases with glassy features.

abstract: A plate withdrawn from a bath of partially wetting liquid entrains a film above a critical velocity. Here, we show that this critical threshold can be substantially increased by the presence of a laminar gas flow opposed to the plate velocity that exerts a tangential shear stress on the liquid-gas interface. Using two-phase immiscible Navier-Stokes simulations and confining the gas to a narrow channel, we derive a closed-form expression for the interfacial stress, which combined with lubrication theory relates the thickness of the film and the contact line velocity to the applied shear stress. As the gas velocity is increased, the film thins and the contact line velocity slows down, until the imposed shear overcomes the drag of the moving plate and entrainment is arrested. As in the quiescent case, the velocity mismatch between plate and contact line is independent of the plate velocity and is set by the applied shear alone. We find that one set of varying gas flow simulations, with constant critical plate velocity, therefore determines the critical gas flow for every smaller plate velocity.

Huaman-Pilco, Elgar Barboza Identifying climatically suitable areas for cacao cultivation (Theobroma cacao L.) is essential to guide sustainable intensification, territorial planning, and compliance with emerging environmental standards in tropical regions. This study assessed the current climatic suitability of cacao in the Amazonas department (northwestern Peru) using an ensemble modeling approach implemented in biomod2, integrating bioclimatic, topographic, and edaphic predictors with spatial biophysical exclusion criteria, legal conservation constraints, regulatory eligibility associated with the European Union Deforestation-Free Products Regulation (EUDR), and local phytosanitary evidence. A total of 403 quality-controlled presence records were used to calibrate multiple machine-learning algorithms under cross-validation, retaining only those with high predictive performance (AUC > 0.9; TSS > 0.7). Decision tree–based models, particularly Random Forest and XGBoost, showed the best individual performance, while the consensus model exhibited greater spatial stability and overall accuracy. Results indicate that approximately 14.8% of the regional territory presents high climatic suitability under current conditions, concentrated in inter-Andean valleys and low- to mid-elevation zones, with thermal seasonality identified as the main environmental predictor. However, the incorporation of territorial and regulatory constraints substantially reduced the effectively available area, especially under the EUDR scenario, demonstrating that cacao expansion potential is strongly conditioned by conservation and regulatory frameworks. High-priority degraded areas emerged as focal opportunities for productive restoration through agroforestry systems. Phytosanitary validation (2021–2024) revealed high spatial concordance between areas of greatest climatic suitability and the prevalence and incidence of major cacao pathogens and pests, particularly Moniliophthora roreri and M. perniciosa, confirming that optimal climatic niches for cultivation also favor biotic pressure. Overall, this study provides an integrative framework combining climatic modeling, territorial management, and phytosanitary risk, delivering robust scientific inputs to inform public policy, land-use planning, and sustainable cacao production strategies in the Amazon.

abstract: Transport networks are key to living and engineered systems. How can transport networks adapt efficiently using only local rules, without a global objective or specific boundary conditions? Inspired by observations in biological transport networks, we adapt networks by subsequently pruning edges by relative resistance, thus removing edges whose resistance is higher than the resistance for routing flow through the rest of the network. We find that adaptation by such a local, boundary-condition-free measure of redundancy, set by topology alone, yields sparse, loop-rich, low-dissipation networks.

abstract: The pronounced chiral asymmetry of biomolecules is a defining feature of living systems, yet the mechanisms by which such asymmetry emerged remain unresolved. Chiral symmetry breaking may have occurred under prebiotic conditions in systems with sufficiently small molecular populations for intrinsic fluctuations to play an important role. Here, we investigate how finite-population fluctuations affect chiral-state selection, the characteristic time for symmetry breaking, and stochastic switching between chiral states in a system driven by autocatalysis and mutual antagonism. We determine how these dynamical processes scale with particle number and derive an analytical expression for the probability of selecting either chiral state as a function of the initial enantiomeric bias. We further calculate the mean selection time for different initial biases and show that, for weak mutual antagonism, fluctuations can induce transitions between opposite chiral states. These results characterize how finite-population fluctuations control both the emergence and stability of molecular chirality in autocatalytic chemical systems.

abstract: The effect of mechanical stresses and deformations upon the behavior and properties of cells and tissues is a topic of paramount interest in the field of biophysics. Its understanding is essential for deepening our comprehension of cellular responses to environmental stimuli, with implications in fields ranging from embryogenesis to tumor development. For boosting the understanding in this field, it is important to develop devices for the application of simple deformations in order to probe the cellular response to the basic mechanical transformations. While a number of stretching devices have been developed, in-plane shearing deformation has been little investigated. Here, a new device is introduced that allows the application of homogeneous in-plane shear upon a cell monolayer while imaging the sample with a commercial optical microscope. A description of the faced experimental challenges is reported and a full characterization is presented. It is demonstrated the capability of the device to apply reproducible, controlled and homogeneous shear of both single cells and confluent cellular monolayers.

abstract: The imbibition of milk into a biscuit provides an example of a broader class of processes in which a liquid invades a porous material, dissolving components of the solid and thereby modifying its own rheology. This coupling between imbibition, dissolution, and evolving fluid rheology also occurs in food processing, filtration, and reactive porous media. While the resulting changes in fluid viscosity are known to affect imbibition, a quantitative description of how this evolving rheology determines the imbibition dynamics is still lacking. Here, we establish such a description for dissolution-driven fluid thickening. For a capillary tube in the well-mixed limit, we derive a generalized Washburn law showing that the evolving viscosity can be incorporated through a rescaled time given by the accumulated inverse viscosity. This predicts a collapse of the imbibition dynamics for different dissolution rates, which we confirm numerically using coupled free-surface and solute-transport simulations. When diffusion is slower, concentration and viscosity become spatially heterogeneous, resulting in a weaker retardation of the advancing liquid than predicted by the well-mixed theory. We then consider disordered porous media and quantify how dissolution-driven thickening and variations in pore geometry affect the dynamics. Our results extend the classical Washburn description to imbibition with evolving fluid properties and provide a quantitative basis for understanding fluid uptake when interactions with the solid progressively modify the rheology of the invading liquid.

abstract: The development of nanostructured antibacterial surfaces has gained significant attention due to the urgent need to combat bacterial colonization and biofouling across food, healthcare, and marine sectors. Among functional metal oxides, zinc oxide (ZnO) nanostructures are particularly promising owing to their rich morphology, favourable physicochemical attributes, and intrinsic bactericidal properties. Here, we utilize a green, eco-friendly Hot Water Treatment (HWT) method to fabricate dense ZnO nanorod arrays on zinc substrates. To overcome the practical limitations and challenges of conventional antibacterial coatings, such as poor operational stability, cytotoxicity, and the risk of antimicrobial resistance, we developed a durable hybrid coating composed of an imidazolium-based ionic liquid stabilized with polydimethylsiloxane. The resulting hybrid-coated nanostructured surfaces exhibit superior antibacterial efficacy against Escherichia coli through a combination of topography-induced mechanical strain and membrane disruption.

abstract: Spatially-resolved mass spectrometry could contribute to the understanding of biological processes. Atom probe tomography (APT) is a technique which could, in principle, fill an analytical gap for nanoscale mass spectrometry. Yet, because of a limited understanding of the process of fragmentation of biomolecules, biological or biochemical interpretation of the obtained data has so far not been successful. Here, we report on analyses of synthetic and biogenic pigmented calcite minerals. The purple coloration of Sphaerechinus granularis sea urchin spines is due to the occlusion of polyhydroxylated naphthoquinone (PHNQ) molecules, mainly spinochrome A, within the calcite phase. Peaks relating to these pigments as well as to other intra-crystalline macromolecules were identified by APT analysis of the purple spine region with comparison to measurements of synthetic calcite single crystals, calcite crystals doped with PHNQ, and the uncoloured (white) region of sea urchin spines. To facilitate the molecular identification of peaks appearing solely in purple-coloured spines, which are possible fragments from PHNQ, we introduce novel APT data filtering techniques based on spatial and temporal correlations in the detection of ions of targeted mass-to-charge state ratios. This allows us to discuss the fragmentation of organic molecules under field conditions and improve the identification of peaks in the mass spectrum, while also determining nanoscale spatial distribution of fragments related to specifically targeted biomolecules in 3D and elucidate the relationship these organic pigment molecules have to the calcite lattice and inorganic elements such as magnesium. The study aims to improve identification of complex molecular structures by APT, including organic molecules, with the potential ability to provide structural information at a near-atomic scale for a range of materials.

abstract: Low affinity chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) can clinically outperform high-affinity variants, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying affinity-dependent activity remain unclear. Here, we show that low CAR affinity enables faster CAR cluster motion, which is central to T-cell activation. We compared low-affinity CAT and high-affinity FMC63 CARs signaling at different stages of activation on supported lipid bilayers functionalized with defined CD19 densities. At low CAR expression on dense CD19 bilayers, low-affinity CAT CARs formed more mature and dynamic synapses, recruited ZAP70 more efficiently, and showed faster microcluster motion. These proximal signaling changes were accompanied by stronger calcium flux and increased NFAT nuclear translocation. Our data support a model in which weaker, lower-affinity CAR-antigen interactions promote receptor turnover, microcluster mobility, and signaling-adaptor recruitment, thereby enhancing downstream signal propagation. Our work provides a mechanistic basis for the superior functional performance reported for affinity-tuned CD19 CAR-T cells.

abstract: We develop a general geometrical framework for growth processes in which the growth rate depends exponentially on the number of active growth-supporting components. The framework separates the fraction of active components from the size of the accessible component space, allowing qualitatively different growth laws to arise from the same underlying construction. Bacterial population growth provides an example of a fixed-size component space controlled primarily by activation and deactivation, whereas examples such as human population growth or speciation provide an expanding component space in which interactions between individuals promote further growth. This motivates a Replicative geometrical law, dX/dt= X exp({beta} X^{gamma}), whose exponent characterizes the scaling of the effective growth-supporting component space and is tested against historical human-population regimes and eukaryotic lineage-through-time data. For innovation indicators such as patents and arXiv manuscript submissions, where an existing item need not itself reproduce, the same construction motivates a Direct Geometrical production law without the prefactor X. The framework therefore provides a common description of fixed and expanding component spaces while distinguishing Replicative from Direct Geometrical growth.

abstract: Shelterin binds telomeres, regulates telomere length, and protects chromosome ends from mis-repair, which is essential for genome stability. Telomere end-protection uniquely depends on the TRF2 subunit, which assembles telomeric DNA into a protective T-loop structure in vivo, yet the biochemical mechanism underlying this process remains unresolved. Using single-molecule optical tweezers and atomic force microscopy, we show that the human shelterin complex tethers distal telomeric DNA repeats, looping the intervening DNA. These bridges withstand tens of piconewtons of applied load, rupture at a force that scales with telomeric repeat number and re-form on relaxation. Structure-function analysis demonstrates that this force-resistant tethering is TRF2-dependent under our conditions and depends on multiple interfaces, with the TRFH domain making a major but non-exclusive contribution: introducing the TRF2 TRFH domain into TRF1 is sufficient to confer tethering, whereas its deletion from TRF2 reduces but does not abolish activity. We propose telomeric dsDNA tethering by TRF2 as a candidate first step in T-loop formation, preceding invasion of the telomeric 3' ssDNA overhang.

abstract: Skeletal dysplasias can occur in animals, including humans, and are attributed to both environmental and genetic causes. As our understanding of the distinguishing phenotypes of different skeletal dysplasias improves, alongside elucidation of the mechanisms and genetic networks that contribute to skeletal development, identifying and controlling genetic mutations in livestock populations has become increasingly possible, including approaches beyond selective breeding alone. Within Scotland an 'achondroplasia' syndrome that was first described in the South Country Cheviot breed of sheep (OMIA 000004-9940), has continued to occur periodically within the same geographical locations, despite culling of affected lambs over many decades. Affected lambs exhibit rounded heads, short legs, a loss of hooves, abnormal stance and short twisted tails. As the condition has been observed in flocks and as progeny from specific ram and ewe matings, and cases have been co-twinned to normal siblings, this suggests a syndrome caused by a recessive genetic condition rather than environmental factors. Through homozygosity mapping and whole genome sequence analyses, we identified a 10 bp deletion in the open reading frame of the PRICKLE1 gene that encodes prickle planar cell polarity protein 1 and is essential for normal vertebrate embryonic development. We identified additional phenotypes present in affected lambs, including a loss of phalanges, neural tube defects, vertebral and articular chondrocyte defects, hair orientation differences and polycystic kidneys, consistent with a loss of PRICKLE1 function based on comparisons to mouse mutant lines. These findings enabled the development of a simple DNA test for the identified PRICKLE1 mutation that was made commercially available to facilitate the elimination of this genetic disease from sheep flocks.

abstract: Phase separating biopolymers are often described by the sticker-spacer model, which accounts for non-attractive linkers that connect discrete attractive moieties. "Associative polymer" theories describe these systems as two coexisting fluids of stickers and spacers, respectively. In such theories the stickers and spacers are decoupled in the sense that sticker binding does not affect spacer conformations or vice versa. Informed by coarse-grained simulations, we develop a phenomenological mean-field theory to determine the microscopic coupling between the sticker and spacer degrees of freedom. Accounting for linkers connecting adjacent spacers introduces free energy contributions due to conformational entropy of the spacer and the binding combinatorics of the stickers. These contributions have opposite dependencies on spacer length because longer spacers allow a greater volume to search for binding partners but incur a greater entropy cost upon bond formation. The length dependent terms from these contributions cancel leaving a length-independent elastic term arising from the fact that a small amount of spacer stretching lowers the free energy by increasing the number of possible binding partners. The cancellation of spacer length from the theory justifies the decoupling approximation and supports mean-field treatments of heterogeneous spacers.

abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) has emerged as an important intermediate in the pathological self-assembly of Tau, yet the molecular mechanisms that regulate this process remain incompletely understood. Although ubiquitin is a prominent component of pathological inclusions in tauopathies and other neurodegenerative diseases, its presence has largely been linked to targeting aberrant proteins for proteasomal or autophagic clearance. Here, we identify Tau as a ubiquitin-binding protein and demonstrate that multivalent, non-covalent ubiquitin recognition regulates multiple stages of Tau self-assembly. Biochemical, biophysical, structural, and computational analyses identified four ubiquitin-binding elements within the Tau microtubule-binding repeat region that engage the canonical hydrophobic patch of ubiquitin, providing a structural basis for multivalent recognition of mono- and poly-ubiquitin species. Functionally, mono- and poly-ubiquitin suppress Tau condensate formation while enhancing the liquid-like properties of condensates that persist. In contrast, mono-ubiquitin selectively enhances aggregation of the disease-linked Tau-P301L variant under conditions without detectable LLPS, demonstrating that ubiquitin exerts distinct effects depending on the molecular context and stage of Tau self-assembly. Together, these findings establish non-covalent ubiquitin recognition as a previously unrecognized mechanism regulating Tau phase behavior and aggregation. More broadly, they expand the role of ubiquitin beyond protein quality control, with ubiquitin architecture providing an additional layer of regulation over Tau condensate formation, dynamics, maturation, and aggregation.

abstract: Long, customizable DNA molecules are an essential tool for in vitro single-molecule biophysics. Most studies still rely on the {lambda}-phage genome, which has a fixed sequence, a non-uniform GC distribution, and limited options for modification. To overcome these limitations, we developed a modular DNA (ModDNA) toolkit that integrates in silico sequence design with cloning, to create long (up to 100 kb) DNA molecules with entirely user-defined sequences. We used a computational workflow with curated databases to design a motif-depleted sequence backbone, into which any desired sequence can be inserted at any position. Golden Gate assembly then builds these sequences into constructs, which we extend iteratively in defined increments up to 100 kb. We show precise placement of local features, e.g. a fluorophore, a bound protein, and a DNA-origami structure, and illustrate the construct's utility in single-molecule visualization assays, including DNA loop extrusion by human condensin I. ModDNA offers a scalable, sequence-programmable alternative to {lambda}-DNA and other restrictive substrates. More broadly, the motif-aware feature-free design connects single-molecule biophysics to emerging efforts in machine-guided regulatory-sequence design and synthetic-genome engineering, where controlled programmable sequence context is increasingly essential.

abstract: The Gene Ontology (GO) is a long-standing knowledge resource that underpins the functional annotation of gene products across numerous biological databases. Released regularly, GO and its associated annotations form a large, continuously evolving dataset whose temporal dynamics have direct consequences for data reuse, versioning, and reproducibility. Because analytical results derived from GO are inherently tied to specific ontology and annotation releases, a systematic understanding of how GO changes over time is essential for transparent interpretation and long-term reuse of GO-based analyses. Here, we present a comprehensive temporal characterization of the Gene Ontology and its annotations spanning 21 years of publicly available releases. Treating successive ontology and annotation versions as longitudinal research data, we quantify changes in ontology structure, term composition, relationships, and annotation content across time and across three representative annotation resources. Our analysis reveals sustained growth of GO over its lifetime, accompanied by marked structural reorganization, particularly affecting high-level, general ontology terms. Notably, across multiple structural metrics, we identify a transition toward increased stability beginning around 2017, consistent with a maturation phase of the resource. This work provides a reference framework for researchers who rely on GO releases for data integration, benchmarking, and reproducible functional analysis.

abstract: Integrative structural biology seeks molecular descriptions consistent with complementary experimental measurements. A particular challenge arises for molecules whose broad conformational ensembles resist description by a few representative structures, such as natively unfolded proteins and fluid-phase biomembrane lipids. Although molecular simulations can generate such ensembles, their simultaneous agreement with a large number of experimental constraints is commonly prevented by model inaccuracies. Here we introduce autofocusing as an approach that integrates experimental information by automated finetuning of the physical model generating the ensemble. We demonstrate it for a fluid bilayer of the phospholipid POPC, for which no existing force field has simultaneously reproduced the complete set of 82 NMR C-H bond order parameters. Autofocusing brings all the 82 within experimental uncertainty while preserving agreement with independent small-angle X-ray scattering measurements and retaining or improving agreement with untargeted NMR relaxation rates and effective correlation times, thus supporting its description of membrane structure and dynamics beyond the calibration targets. The resulting simulations challenge a long-standing two-state interpretation of phosphatidylcholine headgroup structure, instead supporting a broad conformational ensemble poorly represented by crystal-derived conformers. These results establish autofocusing as a practical approach to constructing experimentally grounded conformational ensembles while retaining the computational tractability of classical molecular dynamics.

title: Autofocusing molecular simulations for integrative structural biology of broad conformational ensembles

abstract: Near-term quantum devices remain constrained by limited qubit counts, noise, and shallow circuit depth, restricting their direct application to peptide folding. This work addresses this limitation through a hybrid quantum-classical framework that separates global contact-space exploration from local configuration-space refinement. The pipeline was evaluated on the p53 transactivation peptide. The peptide was encoded using discrete torsional states and Miyazawa-Jernigan contact potentials. Global conformational search was performed using simulated annealing, followed by fragment-level CVaR-based variational quantum eigensolver refinement. Overlapping fragments were stitched and reconstructed into three-dimensional backbone coordinates for structural comparison. Three independent simulated annealing restarts produced negative-energy conformers. The workflow identified a best global conformer at E = -3.70 MJ using simulated annealing. Fragment-level CVaR-VQE refinement generated 30 candidate conformers across three overlapping fragments, the best assembled conformer reaching E = -2.58 MJ after DP stitching and post-stitch refinement. In this trial, the classical SA solution outperformed the VQE-assembled structure and was selected as the final output. The final 65-atom model was successfully reconstructed, but full-backbone alignment against 1YCR yielded an RMSD of 4.65 angstrom, improving to 2.90 angstrom after trimmed alignment. Our work demonstrates a practical quantum-enabled peptide folding workflow for short, flexible peptides, but the present structural accuracy is insufficient for claims of native fold recovery. Its main value is as an auditable framework for testing NISQ-compatible folding strategies.

abstract: Sola l 4.02 is a major tomato allergen of the PR-10 family and a Bet v 1 homolog implicated in pollen–food cross-reactivity, yet its molecular properties remain poorly defined. Here, we report the recombinant production and its comprehensive structural and functional characterization. Sequence and structural analysis support a canonical Bet v 1-like fold including the conserved hydrophobic ligand binding site cavity typical of PR-10 proteins. Biophysical analyses showed that recombinant Sola l 4.02 is a compact, monomeric, and well-folded protein in solution. Circular dichroism measurements revealed moderate thermal stability, with a melting temperature of 57.5 °C and partial recovery of the native conformation after cooling, indicating partially reversible unfolding. The protein remained structurally stable between pH 5.5 and 9.0, whereas mildly acidic conditions promoted partial destabilization. To probe ligand recognition, we tested selected phenolic compounds by microscale thermophoresis. Sola l 4.02 bound quercetin-3-glucoside, naringenin, and daidzein with low micromolar affinities, while caffeic acid showed only weak interaction and hydroxycinnamic acid displayed no detectable binding. Limited proteolysis assays further demonstrated that ligand binding modulates protein susceptibility to digestion. In the presence of bound ligands, Sola l 4.02 displayed enhanced resistance to both trypsin and α-chymotrypsin, with naringenin and daidzein providing the strongest effect. These results identify Sola l 4.02 as a folded, ligand-binding PR-10 allergen whose proteolytic stability is influenced by small-molecule association, providing new insights into the relationship between structural dynamics, ligand occupancy, and the molecular behavior of tomato food allergens.

abstract: Lymphangions, the valved muscular segments of lymphatic vessels, pump lymph against an adverse pressure gradient. Current models resolve this pumping in one vessel, a short chain or a regional network, and whole-body human models are passive. We extend the passive whole-body network of a companion static study to the active regime on the same anatomical graph, with intrinsic contraction, dynamic valves and a respiration-gated venous outlet on every vessel. Without fitting the waveform or the contraction amplitude, the network settles into a bounded pumping cycle at the lymphovenous junction, at a clinical pressure of 7.5 to 12.3 mmHg and a drainage of 35 to 50 mm^3/s. Respiration adds a swing of 1 to 2.5 mmHg at the junction and contraction about 1 mmHg inside the duct. Pressure generation is limited more by load than by drive, and no single contraction amplitude fits every vessel. Raising the subclavian venous pressure from 3 to 15 mmHg lifts the deep cervical node from 8.6 to 21.1 mmHg at the weakest drive, a transmission of 1.04 that falls to 0.78 at the strongest, so contraction buffers cervical drainage against venous pressure. The same solver gives the human cervical outlet pressure that cerebrospinal-fluid drainage models prescribe.

title: An anatomically grounded human-scale dynamic model of contraction-driven lymphatic pumping

abstract: The lymphatic system returns 2 to 3 L of interstitial fluid per day to the venous circulation and drains the central nervous system. Most models of lymph transport describe one lymphangion or a short chain, so they cannot show how body-wide topology, calibre hierarchy and the venous outlet set pressure and flow. We build a passive steady hydraulic model on an anatomically derived graph of the human lymphatic system, with 1010 vertices and 1126 edges expanded to 89,060 sub-edges. Radii follow a Murray cube law, derived both from minimum work and from wall-shear-stress homeostasis. Pressure and flow follow from nodal hydraulic balance over Hagen-Poiseuille conductances, with an exponential wall law, hysteretic valves, Starling leak, node retention and a Windkessel outlet. Active contraction is off, and only the inflow scale is calibrated. Two quantities that are not fitted land in clinical range at the same operating point. Radii fall inside the vessel-class range, from 1.50 mm in the thoracic duct to 0.16 mm in the cervical collectors, and pressures stay below the 50 mmHg cuff scale on all sub-edges. About 49% of the gross load is removed before the outlet, nearly independent of the outflow scale and of the outlet parameters. On the route that drains the central nervous system, 30% of the superficial cervical load reaches the vein, at 10 to 18 mmHg along a segment that cervical-scale models replace with a prescribed outlet pressure. The model is a passive whole-body baseline for contraction-driven and clinical extensions.
authors: Chia-Feng Chang, Ayemon Baraka, Egor Sidorov, Sabee Molloi
title: An anatomically grounded human-scale steady hydraulic model of the lymphatic network

abstract: Neural crest cells (NCCs) provide a well-established system for investigating collective migration during embryonic development and exhibit migratory behaviors with parallels to cancer invasion. Previous studies establish roles for co-attraction, contact inhibition of locomotion, polarity persistence, and tissue confinement in guiding NCC migration. However, it remains unclear whether NCC migration in confined environments occurs through spatial restriction alone or also through a repolarization response induced by contact with boundaries of confinement. By developing a computational model that couples self-generated chemical transport with contact-mediated repolarization and mechanical interactions, we show that cell-boundary contact can reorient cell polarity and sustain directional migration under confinement, whereas no persistent collective direction emerges without confinement. Moreover, suppressing contact-mediated repolarization from non-permissive confinement boundaries while preserving the mechanical interactions prevents sustained directional migration, suggesting that spatial restriction alone is insufficient in the model. Together, these findings establish an experimentally testable mechanism through which self-generated chemical signals and contact with confining tissues jointly regulate collective guidance of NCCs. These insights provide a basis for investigating developmental migration defects and potential strategies to regulate collective tissue invasion.
authors: Aditya Shankar Paspunurwar, Hector Gomez
title: Boundary-contact repolarization provides a mechanism for directional guidance of neural crest cell collectives

abstract: Most systems trained by equilibrium propagation or coupled learning are in the same class as multi-layer perceptrons: while they may be universal function approximators, they struggle to learn associative tasks which are easy for transformers. Equilibrium propagation relies on a bidirectional flow of information through the physical system between input and output. The reverse flow is broken by more complex nonlinear systems, such as those performing multiplication which is needed to express dot-product attention. Here we explicitly restore this bidirectional flow by introducing extra circuit elements for this purpose into a double or dyadic circuit. We then use these ideas to construct an attention mechanism exploiting the exponential current law of sub-threshold MOSFET devices. We show that in simulations this circuit can be trained to perform a simple in-context learning task, despite using realistic reverse components which transmit only an approximate gradient. For this training to succeed we need cross-entropy loss (not mean squared error). We generate nudges appropriate for this loss using a novel floating circuit element, based on the same MOSFET sub-circuit used for softmax. We train the resistors in this circuit using the Lion optimiser, which can be implemented using one capacitor per parameter to store local memory of past gradient estimates.
authors: Michael C. Abbott, Benjamin B. Machta
title: An all-transistor physical-learning transformer can be trained to perform in-context learning

abstract: AI agents can now conduct real-world cyberattacks, scale up capabilities with the number of agents, and collectively pursue misaligned goals to obtain rewards. Together, these factors raise the risk of a population explosion of misaligned agents: agents could compromise computers and secretly deploy additional agents, creating a self-reinforcing cycle where larger populations develop greater collective cyber capability and expand further. This raises a fundamental question: What determines whether a population of misaligned agents remains contained or takes off into this self-reinforcing cycle? This population-level problem is ecological safety: unlike individual-agent or multi-agent safety with a fixed population, it concerns the dynamics of the population itself. Here, we develop an ecological theory of AI-agent populations based on a population growth equation in which fitness (growth rate) depends on cybersecurity capability. We show that, without collaboration, the population takes off only when individual-agent capability exceeds a critical threshold. With collaboration, however, collective cybersecurity capability increases with population size. This creates a critical population threshold: below it, the population declines; above it, the population takes off, even though individual-agent capability has not changed. In ecology, this phenomenon is known as the strong Allee effect. Because red teaming a small group of agents cannot guarantee ecological safety in larger populations, our theory calls for ecological red teaming and population pacing: gradually deploying larger agent populations in controlled environments, while measuring how cyber capability scales with population size, and estimating the critical population size for takeoff. Capability gains may lower this threshold, requiring re-estimation for each new model generation.
authors: Erin Crawley, Hidenori Tanaka
title: Ecology of AI Agents: Collaboration Creates a Population Threshold for Takeoff

abstract: Epithelial tissues play a fundamental role in morphogenesis. Mechanically they can be viewed as thin soft materials exhibiting a solid-fluid duality. The Surface Navier-Stokes-Helfrich model accounts for these properties by combining bending and surface hydrodynamics. In order to account for varying cell thickness we incorporate a thickness field in the spirit of a shallow-water equation, but defined on the (self-)evolving surface. This replaces the inextensibility constraint of the two-dimensional fluid and with it the conservation of surface area by an incompressibility constraint of the thin film fluid allowing for changes in surface area. We develop a numerical scheme based on surface finite elements, perform convergence tests, demonstrate the impact on shape evolution of closed surfaces with a constant enclosed volume and discuss implications on modeling morphogenesis.
authors: Jan Magnus Sischka, Axel Voigt
title: Fluid deformable surfaces with variable thickness - a Surface Shallow-Water-Helfrich model

abstract: The extremely intense pulses of X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs) have enabled imaging of radiation-sensitive samples, such as macromolecular microcrystals, beyond radiation damage limits. These sources have the potential to deliver biomolecular single-particle imaging, similar to cryo-electron microscopy but without the need for cryo-fixation and with temporal resolution from femtoseconds to milliseconds. While this possibility was recognized before XFELs were built, the biological single-particle imaging work-flow has previously only been demonstrated on large virus particles. Based on decades of improvements in X-ray beam focusing, particle delivery, diffraction detection, and advanced analysis, here we demonstrate imaging of a single molecular complex, the giant-hemoglobin erythrocruorin (Ery) with X-ray laser pulses. Two-dimensional classes of diffraction patterns could be reconstructed to 15 Angstrom resolution, and 3D images to approximately 20 Angstrom, while the 3D merged intensity in reciprocal space extended beyond 20 Angstrom. The resolution discrepancy is likely due to heterogeneity caused by gas-phase compaction of the complexes. With increased throughput, this approach could be used to reveal in-situ structural details during mass spectrometry studies of biomolecules, while improvements in sample delivery may provide ultrafast snapshot imaging of biological single-particles in their native-state beyond the limitations of radiation damage.

abstract: The strength of a polymer network is orders of magnitude below that of a polymer chain, because the network concentrates high tension in a small fraction of polymer strands. Here we show that the strength of a network can be greatly amplified by recruiting a larger fraction of strands to bear high tension. We develop approaches to fabricate hydrogels of exceptional strength while maintaining low hysteresis. The strength of the hydrogel increases from ~0.05 MPa for a regular network, to ~1 MPa for a highly entangled network, and further to ~10 MPa for a prestretched interpenetrating network. Similar amplifications of strength are achieved for elastomers. Furthermore, experimental data suggest a scaling relation between strength and strand length. This work provides design principles for creating elastic and strong polymer networks.

abstract: We develop a family of control protocols for finite-time transitions between active nonequilibrium steady states using the noise-color (correlation rate) as the sole control parameter. By reverse-engineering the second moment dynamics of an active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, we determine the time-dependent correlation rate required to realize a prescribed evolution of the system's state. We experimentally implement these protocols with a micrometer-sized optically trapped particle coupled to an engineered active bath, demonstrating transitions substantially faster than the natural relaxation while keeping the confining potential, noise amplitude, and temperature fixed. Our approach extends engineered swift-equilibration methods to far-from-equilibrium steady states by directly controlling the temporal correlations of an active environment. We show how physical constraints impose a speed limit on finite-time transitions, while the freedom in choosing the prescribed system evolution can be exploited to eliminate control discontinuities, minimize the admissible transition time, or optimize a thermodynamic cost.

abstract: The prospect of imaging single biomolecules, viruses and cells with intense, ultrashort X-ray pulses has driven the development of X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs). However, the weak scattering from small particles is easily swamped by background from residual gas, which has so far limited applications to strongly scattering targets such as viruses, cell organelles and cells. Here we report a three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction of an isolated 1-MDa membrane-protein complex, photosystem I (PS I), from single-particle diffraction data. PS I trimers were aerosolised by charge-reduction electrospray ionisation and injected into the European XFEL beam, with partial helium gas exchange reducing background scattering by 80%. From 32 788 diffraction patterns of single trimers in random orientations, we reconstructed the 3D electron density to a resolution of 3.8 nm, limited by the detector geometry. The disc-shaped density, about 22 nm across and 10 nm thick, matches the size of a PS I trimer in a detergent micelle and is consistent with the compaction predicted by molecular dynamics simulations of the complex in vacuo and observed in native mass spectrometry. These results show that membrane-protein complexes can be imaged in vacuo with X-ray lasers, an important step towards ultrafast diffractive imaging of single macromolecules.

abstract: Thermodynamic cycles are the foundation of energy conversion across natural and engineered systems, transforming heat into useful work. However, these cycles traditionally operate between fixed thermal reservoirs, restricting them to specific locations and temperature differences. Here, we introduce autonomous thermodynamic cycles enabled by robotic mobility and sensing, allowing robots to perform thermodynamic cycles by accessing spatially varying temperature fields. We experimentally realize this concept using multistable gas-filled capsules that circulate within the system across a thermal gradient. Our model reveals that rapid transitions in the capsules' energy states allow the system to operate as a mobile heat engine that harvests and stores energy. By linking the capsule-scale internal energy dynamics to the robot's large-scale navigation strategy, we optimize locomotion paths that balance motion cost and energy harvesting. These findings demonstrate that thermodynamic cycles can emerge when autonomous systems navigate their environments, offering an artificial analog of organisms that forage for energy across spatial resources.

abstract: Excitation of absorbing colloids in liquid by pulsed laser irradiation creates highly non-equilibrium states of matter that relax via defined pathways of thermal and non-thermal dissipation channels. The structural fingerprint of these channels can be probed by ultrafast {\it in situ} x-ray scattering methods and classified as a function of temporal delay of excitation excitation density, or specifically laser fluence. We study the example of photo-excitation of a gold colloid by picosecond laser pulses at the interband absorption band at 400 nm in water. By quantifying lattice temperature, crystalline fraction, particle sizes and the structural response of the water around the nanoparticles a reaction map is constructed that allows to pinpoint heating, particle melting, water bubble formation and finally particle fragmentation to form nanoclusters of predominant sizes of < 3 nm for applications in theranostics, photonics or catalysis.
